metadata.title: Being female and being well-situated implies higher performance on creative thinking tests: Evidence across 62 countries from PISA 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata (creative thinking innovative domain plus mathematics and reading) and applies a complex-survey design approach in the effect-size estimation stage. Specifically, for each country/economy and each imputed PV dataset, they run weighted regression models that incorporate student-level sampling weights and replicate weights, using Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) with Fay’s adjustment to obtain robust standard errors under the nested sampling structure (students within schools). Because the analysis is a two-stage individual-participant meta-analytic framework (country-specific regressions followed by meta-analysis), weights are used to support population-representative inference rather than to train an ML predictor. The manuscript does not name the exact weight variable(s) (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states the use of sampling and replicate weights consistent with PISA’s complex design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used a subset of PISA 2022 publicly available OECD data, restricting to the 62 of 64 country/economy samples that include creative thinking (innovative domain). Excluded Cyprus because no creative thinking data were available, and excluded Costa Rica because SES variables were not available. Removed a very small amount of missingness for the binary gender variable via listwise deletion (n=74). For PVs (mathematics, reading, creative thinking), removed rows with missing PV data in Iceland (n=4) via listwise deletion because completeness across PVs was otherwise available and the rows were treated as corrupted. For ESCS missingness, applied nested multiple imputation (M=10) per country and per PV set, using a Bayesian substantive-model-compatible approach with science competence as an auxiliary variable in the covariate model.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (innovative domain; 15-year-olds; country/economy level meta-analysis)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking (PVs) — gender main effect (Gender coded 0=female, 1=male)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis (Table 1): Gender estimate = -0.277 (SE=0.014), p<0.001; 95% CI [-0.304, -0.250]; 95% prediction interval [-0.472, -0.081]; heterogeneity τ²=0.009, I²=87.43%. Additional analysis (Creative thinking (PVs) — SES main effect (ESCS z-standardized)): Cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis (Table 1): SES estimate = 0.334 (SE=0.009), p<0.001; 95% CI [0.315, 0.353]; 95% prediction interval [0.192, 0.476]; heterogeneity τ²=0.005, I²=89.52%. Additional analysis (Creative thinking (PVs) — Gender × SES interaction): Cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis (Table 1): Gender*SES estimate = -0.034 (SE=0.005), p<0.001; 95% CI [-0.044, -0.023]; 95% prediction interval [-0.088, 0.021]; heterogeneity τ²=0.000, I²=46.84%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking the study leveraged Gender, socioeconomic status (ESCS), and their interaction to estimate gender differences in creative thinking plausible values, finding that female students outperformed male students (Gender estimate = -0.277, p<0.001). This indicates that gender disparities in creative thinking favor girls and that creative-thinking support policies should be designed to reduce male underperformance while recognizing substantial cross-country heterogeneity.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics (core domain; 15-year-olds; country/economy level meta-analysis)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis (Table 1): Gender estimate = 0.028 (SE=0.015), p=0.074; 95% CI [-0.003, 0.058]; 95% prediction interval [-0.198, 0.253]; heterogeneity τ²=0.012, I²=93.68%. Additional analysis (Mathematics (PVs) — SES main effect (ESCS z-standardized)): Cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis (Table 1): SES estimate = 0.361 (SE=0.010), p<0.001; 95% CI [0.342, 0.381]; 95% prediction interval [0.213, 0.510]; heterogeneity τ²=0.005, I²=92.79%. Additional analysis (Mathematics (PVs) — Gender × SES interaction): Cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis (Table 1): Gender*SES estimate = -0.006 (SE=0.006), p<0.001; 95% CI [-0.018, 0.006]; 95% prediction interval [-0.066, 0.054]; heterogeneity τ²=0.001, I²=54.45%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics the study leveraged Gender, socioeconomic status (ESCS), and their interaction to estimate gender differences in mathematics plausible values, finding no statistically substantial overall gender effect (Gender estimate = 0.028, p=0.074) despite high between-country heterogeneity (τ²=0.012). This indicates that mathematics gender gaps are context-dependent and that policy should focus on system-level drivers of where boys or girls outperform rather than assuming a uniform gender pattern.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Reading (core domain; 15-year-olds; country/economy level meta-analysis)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis (Table 1): Gender estimate = -0.294 (SE=0.014), p<0.001; 95% CI [-0.322, -0.256]; 95% prediction interval [-0.501, -0.087]; heterogeneity τ²=0.011, I²=92.07%. Additional analysis (Reading (PVs) — SES main effect (ESCS z-standardized)): Cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis (Table 1): SES estimate = 0.342 (SE=0.009), p<0.001; 95% CI [0.324, 0.361]; 95% prediction interval [0.205, 0.479]; heterogeneity τ²=0.005, I²=90.78%. Additional analysis (Reading (PVs) — Gender × SES interaction): Cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis (Table 1): Gender*SES estimate = -0.026 (SE=0.006), p<0.001; 95% CI [-0.037, -0.015]; 95% prediction interval [-0.085, 0.033]; heterogeneity τ²=0.001, I²=52.77%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Reading the study leveraged Gender, socioeconomic status (ESCS), and their interaction to estimate gender differences in reading plausible values, finding that female students outperformed male students (Gender estimate = -0.294, p<0.001). This indicates that reading instruction and literacy support should continue to address persistent male underperformance, while accounting for substantial cross-country variability in effect sizes.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 microdata for 62 countries/economies (N=493,660 students) using an integrative two-stage individual-participant meta-analytic approach. It estimates country-specific regression effects on PISA plausible values for creative thinking (innovative domain), mathematics, and reading, then meta-analyzes the standardized coefficients using cluster-robust random-effects models with BRR/Fay replicate-weight variance estimation. Missing ESCS values are handled via nested multiple imputation (M=10) compatible with the subsequent effect-size regressions, and PVs are combined using Rubin’s rules. Across domains, female students outperform male students in creative thinking and reading (e.g., creative thinking gender estimate = -0.277, p<0.001), while SES shows strong positive associations with performance (creative thinking SES estimate = 0.334, p<0.001). The paper reports heterogeneity (e.g., high I² for gender effects) and tests macro moderators (OECD membership, HDI, GGGI, power distance), finding creative-thinking disparities largely stable across contexts. Limitations include reliance on observational cross-sectional PISA data and the fact that the approach is not ML predictive modeling despite ML-related framing in the venue.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is an integrative individual-participant meta-analysis using regression-based effect-size estimation and meta-regression, not a machine-learning predictive modeling study. Consequently, no ML algorithms (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost) are trained or compared, so ml_techniques.primary and all_techniques are intentionally left empty. The outcomes are reported as standardized regression coefficients and heterogeneity statistics from meta-analytic models rather than ML performance metrics.
